messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Bartender
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mina, a 30-year-old Middle Eastern woman, came to treatment several years after leaving a marriage that had felt to her, in some quiet and familiar way, like a life built around monitoring danger. She had grown up in a home where domestic violence was witnessed repeatedly as a child, scenes of shouting, sudden movement, and bodies crowding doorways becoming part of the background of daily life. Even now, she struggled to tell that history in a smooth, linear way. When asked about it, she would pause, look down, and say that she knew what had happened, but that the frightening parts did not come out in words. At times the memory would rise so sharply that she had to stop speaking altogether, her face tightening and her breathing changing as if the scene were happening again in the room with her. What she could describe was fragmentary: the sense of being small and trapped in the household space, the abruptness of movements that could turn an ordinary moment into something dangerous, and the lasting impression that people closest to you could not be counted on to behave safely.

As a child, Mina learned to keep herself quiet and contained, and as an adult she had come to believe that she could not rely on herself either. She often doubted whether she would do the right thing, describing a chronic mistrust in her own judgment that made decisions feel heavier than they seemed to other people. That self-doubt carried into her marriage and later into her divorce, though she did not present the divorce as a separate trauma so much as part of a longer pattern in which she had tried to make herself smaller and more controlled. She described making herself “very careful” with her feelings, trying hard not to show much emotion because once she started, she feared it would spill over and she would lose control. In session she spoke in a measured, restrained way, as if keeping a tight lid on her reaction were something she needed to do to stay safe.

In the years after leaving home, Mina developed a set of habits that made sense to her as preparation. She mentally rehearsed worst-case scenarios so she would not be caught off guard, running through what she would do if someone suddenly came toward her, if an argument broke out, or if she found herself unable to get out quickly. At home she repeatedly checked doors and windows, sometimes returning to them several times after already making sure they were locked. She said it was the only way she could settle enough to sit down. Even then, she felt safe in only a very limited number of places, and wide-open or exposed spaces were especially hard for her. She described open spaces not simply as uncomfortable but as places where she felt vulnerable and too visible, where there was nowhere to orient herself if something changed too quickly.

Her work as a bartender made some of these experiences difficult to hide. The bar was often busy, with people moving fast behind her and around her, and sudden gestures from customers or coworkers would put her immediately on guard. A hand reaching across the counter too quickly, a person stepping in too close, or a chair scraping back abruptly could make her body tense before she had time to think. She did her best to control her expression so that none of this showed, but she left shifts feeling drained from holding herself so tightly together. There were also moments when she could not help noticing how much the open layout of some evenings, especially when the bar felt crowded and exposed, unsettled her. She kept track of exits, trusted only a few familiar corners, and preferred settings where she could see who was coming and going.

By the time she sought help, Mina was no longer only managing old memories but living inside them in a practical, everyday sense. She was afraid of sudden movement, afraid of being in the wrong place without warning, and afraid of her own uncertainty when she had to make decisions quickly. She wanted therapy because the checking, the vigilance, and the effort to keep her emotions contained had become exhausting, and because she was tired of feeling that other people could not be trusted. More than anything, she hoped to feel less trapped by the sense that danger might appear at any moment, and to find some way of living that did not require her to rehearse catastrophe every day just to get through it.
